Proposal Number: BIO-2024-07821
Program: Ecosystem Science
Program Officer: Dr. Katherine Wells
Submission Date: October 15, 2024
Project Information
Project Title: Alpine Ecosystem Response to Climate Change in the Northern Rockies
Principal Investigator: Dr. Sarah Chen
Co-PI: Dr. Michael Torres
Institution: University of Idaho
Department: Department of Biological Sciences
Requested Amount: $485,000
Project Period: September 1, 2025 - August 31, 2028
Sponsoring Agency: National Science Foundation
Project Abstract
This project investigates the impacts of climate change on alpine ecosystems in the Northern Rocky Mountains.
Our research combines long-term field monitoring, remote sensing, and ecological modeling to understand how
rising temperatures, shifting precipitation patterns, and changing snowpack dynamics affect plant community
composition, soil microbial diversity, and ecosystem carbon cycling. The study will establish 24 permanent
monitoring plots across an elevational gradient (2,200-3,100m) in the Sawtooth and White Cloud mountain
ranges.

Broader Impacts
This project will train 4 graduate students and 8 undergraduate researchers in alpine ecology and climate
science. Results will be shared with the Sawtooth National Recreation Area and the U.S. Forest Service to inform
land management decisions. We will develop educational materials for Idaho high school science teachers,
reaching an estimated 500 students per year through a summer workshop program.

FOA Number: PA-23-152
Study Section: Neurotransporters, Receptors, and Calcium Signaling (NTRC)
Funding Mechanism: R01 - Research Project Grant
Submission Date: February 5, 2024
Project Information
Project Title: Neural Circuit Mechanisms of Working Memory in Prefrontal Cortex
Principal Investigator: Dr. James Park
Degree: Ph.D.
Institution: University of Idaho
Department: Department of Biological Sciences - Neuroscience Program
Total Budget: $1,250,000
Project Period: July 1, 2024 - June 30, 2029
Sponsoring Agency: National Institutes of Health
Human Subjects: No
Vertebrate Animals: Yes - Mouse model (Mus musculus)
Clinical Trial: No
Specific Aims
Aim 1: Characterize the firing patterns of prefrontal cortex (PFC) neurons during working memory tasks using
two-photon calcium imaging in head-fixed mice.
Aim 2: Determine the causal role of PFC-to-hippocampal projections in working memory maintenance using
optogenetic manipulation.
Aim 3: Develop a computational model of PFC circuit dynamics that predicts working memory capacity from
neural population activity patterns.

Research Strategy
Working memory, the ability to transiently hold and manipulate information, is fundamental to cognition. Deficits
in working memory are observed in schizophrenia, ADHD, and age-related cognitive decline. Despite decades of
research, the circuit-level mechanisms by which prefrontal cortex (PFC) neurons maintain persistent activity
during working memory remain poorly understood.
This project employs state-of-the-art two-photon calcium imaging to record the activity of hundreds of PFC
neurons simultaneously in behaving mice performing a delayed non-match-to-sample task. Combined with
optogenetic manipulation of specific projection pathways and computational modeling, we aim to provide a
comprehensive understanding of how PFC circuits support working memory.
Vertebrate Animals
All procedures will be performed in accordance with the NIH Guide for the Care and Use of Laboratory Animals
and approved by the University of Idaho IACUC (Protocol #2024-015). We will use approximately 200 adult
C57BL/6J mice (both sexes, 8-12 weeks old) over the project period. Mice will be housed in the university
vivarium with standard 12h light/dark cycles and ad libitum food and water access.

Project Information
Project Title: Alpine Ecosystem Response to Climate Change in the Northern Rockies
Principal Investigator: Dr. Sarah Chen
Co-PI: Dr. Michael Torres
Institution: University of Idaho
Department: Department of Biological Sciences
Requested Amount: $485,000
Project Period: September 1, 2025 - August 31, 2028
Sponsoring Agency: National Science Foundation
Project Abstract
This project investigates the impacts of climate change on alpine ecosystems in the Northern Rocky Mountains.
Our research combines long-term field monitoring, remote sensing, and ecological modeling to understand how
rising temperatures, shifting precipitation patterns, and changing snowpack dynamics affect plant community
composition, soil microbial diversity, and ecosystem carbon cycling. The study will establish 24 permanent
monitoring plots across an elevational gradient (2,200-3,100m) in the Sawtooth and White Cloud mountain
ranges.
